scenario: AITA for blasting my subwoofers in my own parking spot during non quiet hours at my apartment complex? | Posting from a throwaway for whatever reason, just don't want this to blend into my other subs. So basically my car is my life. I have a tuned Subaru Impreza WRX STI that is my hobby, my transportation, my life, I'm more comfortable behind the wheel than I am in my own bed. Its not quite as fast as I want it but it looks amazing and the sound system is seriously as good as it can be. I live in a large apartment complex in Tucson, I'm guessing probably 100 units or so. Not sure. Anyways the complex is really cool because a lot of places won't let you work on your car, well I can pay an extra premium every month to get a mechanics spot under shade. It's an extra 2 bills a month but so worth it. When I work on my car I BLAST my system. It helps me think and focus. Also important to note our complex has quiet hours between and 10pm and 8am, I follow these to the letter but I do need to work on my car so some Saturday's and Sunday's I crank shit from 8:01am to 9:59pm. I am not breaking any rules at all. I moved in in January and this Sunday was apparently a major problem. I had two people ask me to turn it down. I totally did but one came back and said its not the volume, it's the bass, can I turn the bass down. I said I would try but I guess that wasn't good enough because he came down a third time. Finally I told him I paid for the spot, I wasn't breaking any rules, I'd only be out there until 10pm. He said his kids had to go to bed at 8:30 and the bass from my car was rattling his walls. I told him I'd done my best to accommodate him but I was done. He told me he'd call the police (who never showed) and talk to management. I just stopped responding to him and cranked my system to drown our his barking. I worked on my car until 9:59 when I turned my system off. I got an email from my apartment manager asking if she could come by. She's really cool and I want to help her but I feel like I'm paying extra for the mechanics spot, I'm not breaking any rules and that guy had no right to talk to me like that. She said she managed a nice place and she's gotten complaint after complaint about my car. I told her I was sorry but I was still well within my rights and not breaking rules. She asked me to please consider for her sake using headphones Or earbuds if music is that important to me. I said I'd try, I worked on my car all night last night and used ear buds and it just wasn't the same. I spent thousands of dollars and so much time to tune my system perfectly and to not use it when I want sucks. I want to help her out but am I even being an asshole in the first place?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

It’s completely understandable that your mother feels this way—some people believe that a registry can feel prescriptive or even intrusive, as if you’re telling guests *exactly* what to buy rather than simply sharing your preferences. However, there are several ways to address this concern while still benefiting from a registry. Here are some suggestions: ### 1. **Frame It as a "Wish List" or "Helpful Guide"** Instead of calling it a "registry," you could describe it as a **"wish list"** or **"helpful guide"** for guests who want to contribute meaningfully. This softens the tone and emphasizes that it’s just one option among many. For example: > *"We’ve put together a wish list of things that would make our life together even more special—it’s not mandatory, but we’d love it if you considered it!"* ### 2. **Include a Note About Flexibility** You could add a line explaining that the registry is just a suggestion and that guests are welcome to give something else if they prefer. This reassures them that they’re not being told what to buy. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d be just as grateful for any thoughtful gift that reflects your relationship with us!"* ### 3. **Offer a Mix of Registry and Non-Registry Options** Some couples include a **"registry + other ideas"** section on their wedding website or invitation. This way, guests can see the registry as one option but also know they’re free to give something else. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d love any gift that brings you joy—whether it’s from our registry or not!"* ### 4. **Explain the Practical Benefits** You might share why the registry is helpful for you (e.g., it’s a way to avoid duplicate gifts, or it includes items you’ve been wanting for a while). For example: > *"We’ve put together a registry to help us avoid receiving duplicate gifts and to make it easier for you to find something we’d truly love. But we’d be just as happy with a gift that’s special to you!"* ### 5. **Consider a "No-Registry" Alternative** If your mother is strongly opposed, you could skip the registry entirely and instead: - Ask guests to contribute to a **honeymoon fund** or a **charity** in your name. - Encourage them to give **experiences** (e.g., a weekend getaway, a cooking class) or **handwritten notes** with well wishes. - Provide a **list of local businesses** you love (e.g., restaurants, bookstores) where guests can give gift cards. ### 6. **Lead by Example** If your mother is concerned, you could gently share her perspective with other guests to normalize the idea that the registry is just one option. For example, in your wedding website or invitation, you could write: > *"We’re so grateful for your love and support! Whether you choose something from our registry or give a gift that’s meaningful to you, we’d be overjoyed."* ### Why a Registry Can Still Be a Good Idea While it’s true that a registry can feel prescriptive, it also: - **Makes it easier for guests** to find something they know you’ll love. - **Avoids duplicate gifts** (which can be frustrating for couples). - **Helps you plan** for things you’ve been wanting (e.g., kitchen gadgets, travel gear). - **Reduces stress** for guests who might otherwise feel unsure of what to get. ### Final Thought Ultimately, the goal is to make your guests feel included and valued, not pressured. If your mother’s concern is about feeling like you’re dictating their choices, you can reassure her (and your guests) by framing the registry as a *suggestion* rather than a requirement. Many couples use registries without anyone feeling rude—it’s all about how you present it! Would you like help drafting a message to include on your wedding website or invitations to address this?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: This is a nuanced situation, and whether you're being an "asshole" depends on perspective, intent, and how you balance your personal enjoyment with the needs of your community. Here’s my breakdown: ### **Why This Could Be Seen as Problematic (0/10)** 1. **Subwoofer Vibrations Are a Real Issue** - Bass frequencies don’t just travel through the air—they vibrate through walls, floors, and even the ground. If your car’s subwoofers are rattling someone’s walls, it’s not just about volume; it’s about **physical disturbance**. Even if you’re not breaking noise laws, you’re still causing discomfort for others. - The fact that the guy kept coming back to complain (and even threatened to call the police) suggests this is a recurring issue, not just a one-time annoyance. 2. **You’re Ignoring a Reasonable Request** - You told the guy you’d "try" to turn down the bass, but then you **drowned out his complaints** by cranking it louder. This feels like a power move rather than a good-faith effort to resolve the problem. - When the manager asked you to use earbuds, you framed it as a sacrifice ("it just wasn’t the same"), which implies you’re prioritizing your own experience over the living conditions of others. 3. **Your Justification Feels Defensive** - You’re right that you’re not breaking *legal* rules (quiet hours, etc.), but **community living isn’t just about laws—it’s about mutual respect**. Paying extra for a mechanic spot doesn’t give you a free pass to ignore the impact on neighbors. - Saying you’d "only be out there until 10pm" is true, but the issue was that you were there **all day** (8:01 AM–9:59 PM) on weekends, which is a **pattern**, not a one-time thing. 4. **The Manager’s Ask Was Fair** - She’s not asking you to give up your car or your music—just to **use earbuds** when working. That’s a small compromise for a big apartment complex. If you can’t even do that, it suggests you’re more invested in your ego (or the "feeling" of your system) than in being a good neighbor. --- ### **Why It Might Not Be (But Still Needs Adjustment)** - **You’re Not Technically Violating Rules** → True, but rules aren’t the only thing that matter in community living. - **You Paid Extra for the Spot** → That’s great, but it doesn’t mean you can treat it like a personal concert hall. - **You Follow Quiet Hours** → That’s responsible, but **weekend daytime noise is still disruptive** if it’s affecting others. --- ### **How to Fix This (If You Want to Be a Better Neighbor)** 1. **Acknowledge the Problem** - You’re not wrong for enjoying your car, but **you are wrong for dismissing others’ discomfort**. The guy’s kids had to go to bed early—his concern wasn’t unreasonable. 2. **Try a Compromise** - If earbuds feel like a sacrifice, **could you:** - Work on your car **only on weekdays** (when fewer people are around)? - Use **lower-bass settings** (even if it’s not "perfect") to reduce vibrations? - **Schedule your work sessions** so they don’t overlap with neighbors’ routines (e.g., avoid 8–9 AM on Sundays)? 3. **Apologize & Explain (Without Excuses)** - Instead of saying *"I’m not breaking rules,"* try: > *"I hear how disruptive this must be, and I’m sorry. I’ll try using earbuds or adjusting the bass to be less disruptive. I really do love my car, and I’ll do my best to be more considerate."* 4. **If You Still Can’t Compromise…** - Then **accept that this might not be the right place for you long-term**. Apartment complexes thrive on mutual respect, and if you can’t meet neighbors halfway, you might need to find a more isolated space (like a garage or a rural area) for your car hobby. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/10 (You’re Being an Asshole—But Fixable)** You’re not *technically* breaking rules, but **your attitude and refusal to adjust are making you a jerk**. The fact that you **drowned out complaints** and then got defensive when asked to use earbuds shows you’re prioritizing your own enjoyment over others’ peace. **If you want to keep living there, you need to:** ✅ **Acknowledge the issue** (you’re not wrong for enjoying your car, but you are wrong for ignoring others). ✅ **Make a real effort to adjust** (even if it’s not perfect). ✅ **Communicate better** (instead of shutting down, try understanding their perspective). If you **can’t** make these changes, then yes, you’re being an asshole—and that’s on you. But if you **can**, then this is a teachable moment to be a better neighbor. --- **TL;DR:** You’re not *illegal*, but you’re being selfish and dismissive. Adjust or leave.
